Moses ... chosen--</hi>both what they were by divine choice (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.70">Psa 78:70</reference>). <div eID="gen10306" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b52cd6b8011cf3679525df48b4938c486626eb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6724"/><div sID="gen10307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6724"/><hi type="bold">27. signs--</hi>literally, "words of signs," or rather, as "words" in Hebrew means "things," "things of His signs," that is, His marvellous tokens of power (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.5">Psa 145:5</reference>, Margin). Compare the same Hebraism (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.3">Psa 65:3</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen10307" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a89b8048b0e301f3705bc8e72c5063c86174ef0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6725"/><div sID="gen10308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6725"/>28-36. The ninth plague is made prominent as peculiarly wonderful.<div eID="gen10308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they rebelled not--</hi>Moses and Aaron promptly obeyed God (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.27">He 11:27</reference>); (compare Ex 7:<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.10">1-11:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.78.44-Ps.78.51">Psa 78:44-51</reference>, with which this summary substantially agrees). Or, rather, the "darkness" here is figurative (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.16">Jr 13:16</reference>), the literal plague of darkness (<reference osisRef="Exod.10.22">Ex 10:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.10.23">23</reference>) being only alluded to as the symbol of God's wrath which overhung Egypt as a dark cloud during all the plagues. Hence, it is placed first, out of the historical order. Thus, "They rebelled not (that is, no longer) against His word," refers to the Egyptians. Whenever God sent a plague on them, they were ready to let Israel go, though refusing when the plague ceased.<div eID="gen10309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his word--</hi>His command to let Israel go [Hengstenberg]. Of the ten plagues, only eight are mentioned, the fifth, the murrain of beasts, and the sixth, the boils, being omitted. <div eID="gen10310" type="x-p"/>
entries.837db0ce29c220c38dbe2e7d17ba2bd0951d85b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6731"/><div sID="gen10317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6731"/><hi type="bold">37. with silver and gold--</hi>presented them by the Egyptians, as an acknowledgment due for their labors in their bondage (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.12.35">Ex 12:35</reference>).<div eID="gen10317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one feeble person--</hi>or, "stumbler," unfit for the line of march. Compare "harnessed," that is, accoutred and marshalled as an army on march (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.18">Ex 13:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.27">Is 5:27</reference>). <div eID="gen10318" type="x-p"/>
entries.188324b3d41227d832dcb5c63e18a05a67f2d83a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6732"/><div sID="gen10319" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6732"/>38. (Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.12.33">Ex 12:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.25">De 11:25</reference>). <div eID="gen10319" type="x-p"/>
entries.1de39844221fdea3d1fdb54405efd8959a655c0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6733"/><div sID="gen10320" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6733"/><hi type="bold">39. covering--</hi>in sense of protection (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.13.21">Ex 13:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.10.34">Nu 10:34</reference>). In the burning sands of the desert the cloud protected the congregation from the heat of the sun; an emblem of God's protecting favor of His people, as interpreted by Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Is 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Num.9.16">Nu 9:16</reference>). <div eID="gen10320" type="x-p"/>
entries.4193c6ecafee82d9aa6422dc12022de0a17080e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6734"/><div sID="gen10321" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6734"/>42-45. The reasons for these dealings: (1) God's faithfulness to His covenant, "His holy promise" of Canaan, is the fountain whence flowed so many acts of marvellous kindness to His people (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.105.8">Psa 105:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.11">11</reference>). <reference osisRef="Exod.2.24">Ex 2:24</reference> is the fundamental passage [Hengstenberg]. (2) That they might be obedient. The observance of God's commands by Abraham was the object of the covenant with him (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Ge 18:19</reference>), as it was also the object of the covenant with Israel, that they might observe God's statutes.<div eID="gen10321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remembered ... and Abraham--</hi>or, "remembered His holy word (that is, covenant confirmed) with Abraham." <div eID="gen10322" type="x-p"/>

entries.8ef9c271dc7138e147b0c28c383c94736e31eefd: <div eID="gen22138" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22139" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22140" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22140" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22139" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22141" type="x-p"/> An exhortation to praise God for his wondrous works, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.1-Psa.105.5">Psa 105:1-5</reference>; his goodness to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.6-Psa.105.16">Psa 105:6-16</reference>; to Joseph in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.17-Psa.105.22">Psa 105:17-22</reference>; to Israel in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.23-Psa.105.25">Psa 105:23-25</reference>; to Moses in the same land, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.26">Psa 105:26</reference>; the plagues sent on the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.27-Psa.105.36">Psa 105:27-36</reference>; the deliverance of the Israelites out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.37">Psa 105:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.38">Psa 105:38</reference>; how he supported them in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.39-Psa.105.43">Psa 105:39-43</reference>; and brought them into Canaan, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.44">Psa 105:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.105.45">Psa 105:45</reference>. <div eID="gen22141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22142" type="x-p"/> We find several verses of this Psalm in 1 Chronicles 16, from which it is evident that David was the author of the principal part of it: but it was probably enlarged and sung at the restoration of the people from the Babylonish captivity. The hallelujah which terminates the preceding Psalm, is made the title of this by the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic: but it has no title either in the Hebrew or Chaldee. The Syriac considers it a paraphrase on the words, "Fear not, Jacob, to go down into Egypt; and teach us spiritually not to fear when we are obliged to contend with devils; for God is our shield, and will fight for us." The Psalm is a history of God's dealings with Abraham and his posterity, till their settlement in the promised land. <div eID="gen22142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22143" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22144" type="x-p"/> O give thanks - He had been meditating on God's gracious dealings with their fathers; and he calls upon himself and all others to magnify God for his mercies.
entries.3d7c426e5dedaf042363cc986f0cd7e42be15216: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22145" type="x-p"/> Talk ye of all his wondrous works - נפלאתיו niphleothaiv, "of his miracles." Who have so many of these to boast of as Christians! Christianity is a tissue of miracles; and every part of the work of grace on the soul is a miracle. Genuine Christian converts may talk of miracles from morning to night; and they should talk of them, and recommend to others their miracle-working God and Savior.
entries.9c327537046cabb9cda7c54e71bf9a77a0affc1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22146" type="x-p"/> Glory ye in his holy name - Show the name Jesus: exult in it - praise it. His name was called Jesus; because he came to save his people from their sins. <div eID="gen22146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22147" type="x-p"/> Let the heart of them rejoice - That is, the heart of those shall rejoice who seek the Lord: therefore it is added: -
entries.a82f4dc365136405468618773ac1d036890c97bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22148" type="x-p"/> Seek the Lord - Worship the one only Supreme Being, as the only and all-sufficient good for the soul of man. <div eID="gen22148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22149" type="x-p"/> And his strength - Man is weak; and needs connection with the strong God that he may be enabled to avoid evil and do good. <div eID="gen22149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22150" type="x-p"/> Seek his face - Reconciliation to him. Live not without a sense of his favor. <div eID="gen22150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22151" type="x-p"/> Evermore - Let this be thy chief business. In and above all thy seeking, seek this.
entries.13e680a1d04354b980238a564756460b4e43eabb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen22151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22152" type="x-p"/> Remember his marvellous works - Keep up communion with thy Maker, that thou mayest neither forget him nor his works. <div eID="gen22152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22153" type="x-p"/> The judgments of his mouth - Whatsoever he has spoken concerning good or evil. His commands, promises, threatenings; and particularly what he has foretold, and what he has done.
entries.c5a520ef39cac1cc9773532c0ad95d289b956c51: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen22153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22154" type="x-p"/> O ye seed of Abraham - Ye Jews especially, who have been the peculiar objects of the Divine favor.
entries.0e6e135f0879f385dbf5db8f6b776f17689a95b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22155" type="x-p"/> He is the Lord our God - He is Jehovah, the self-existent and eternal God. He is our God, he is our portion; has taken us for his people, and makes us happy in his love. <div eID="gen22155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22156" type="x-p"/> The following abstract of the history of the Israelites presents but few difficulties. See the notes on Psalm 78 (note).
entries.83e70abaa65db447475b6368c4dcd21d6346ca29: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen22156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22157" type="x-p"/> But a few men - When all appearances were against them, and nothing but the arm of God could have brought them through their difficulties, and given them a settlement in the promised land.
entries.731a0a3d57407c126a34397c47e62615135c9764: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen22157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22158" type="x-p"/> When they went from one nation to another - From several circumstances in the history of the travels of the ancient Hebrews, we find that the wilderness through which they then passed was well peopled.
entries.7984674361eeb3c34f185139c597dcc3740c8b40: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen22158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22159" type="x-p"/> Touch not mine anointed - It is supposed that the patriarchs are here intended; but the whole people of Israel may be meant. They were a kingdom of priests and kings unto God; and prophets, priests, and kings were always anointed.
entries.737b03077e7dc7f13a0859f94ea2942cad6cd196: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen22159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22160" type="x-p"/> Until the time that his word came - This appears to refer to the completion of Joseph's interpretation of the dreams of the chief butler and baker. <div eID="gen22160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22161" type="x-p"/> The Word of the Lord tried him - This seems to refer to the interpretation of Pharaoh's dreams, called אמרת יהוה imrath Yehovah, "the oracle of the Lord," because sent by him to Pharaoh. See <reference osisRef="Gen.41.26">Gen 41:26</reference>, and Kennicott in loco.
entries.177a55c725fa25ed7851239e23a9df5b1c5cdb97: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen22161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22162" type="x-p"/> He turned their heart - "Their heart was turned." So the Syriac and Arabic. After befriending the Hebrews on Joseph's account, to whom they were so deeply indebted, finding them to multiply greatly in the land, and at last to become more powerful than the Egyptians themselves, they turned their attention to the adoption of measures, in order to prevent the Hebrews from possessing themselves of the government of the whole land; they curtailed them of their privileges, and endeavored to depress them by all possible means, and by a variety of legal enactments. This appears to be the sole meaning of the phrase, "He turned their heart;" or, "their heart was turned."
entries.354db713da6394b54ab227a107905ddbd7576177: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen22162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22163" type="x-p"/> They showed his signs - Here is a reference to the plagues with which God afflicted the Egyptians. See Exodus 7-12 (note), <reference osisRef="Psa.78.43">Psa 78:43</reference> (note), and the notes on them.
entries.211330caef319588602cecefb4329fae586b7ecf: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen22163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22164" type="x-p"/> They rebelled not against his word - Instead of ולא מרו velo maru, "they rebelled," some think that a ש shin has been lost from before the word, and that it should be read ולא שמרו velo shamru, "they did not observe or keep his word." Or the words may be spoken of Moses and Aaron; they received the commandment of God, and they did not rebel against it. They believed what he had spoken, and acted according to his orders. It could not be spoken of the Egyptians; for they rebelled against his words through the whole course of the transactions.
entries.d7f3131e5ef81e8e77c6c606124d3083a3867bb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen22164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22165" type="x-p"/> He smote their vines also, and their fig trees - This is not mentioned in Exodus; but we have had it before, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.47">Psa 78:47</reference>.
entries.14c73b9fecb7be5e6fa71b1636602f973b239e0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen22165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22166" type="x-p"/> He opened the rock, and the waters rushed out - See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.17.6">Exo 17:6</reference>, to which I can now add, that a piece of this rock, broken off by the hand of my nephew, E. S. A. Clarke, in the course of the present year [1822,] now lies before me. It is fine granite; and so well distinguished as a granite, that the feldt-spar, the mica, and the quartz, of which granite is composed, appear very distinctly. It is worthy of remark, that, as granite is supposed, in the most accredited systems of geology, to be the very basis of the earth, the original rock, and all other substances to be superimpositions upon it, and as the decompositions of the feldt-spar produce pure vegetable earth, this rock should be used for this purpose, and should be an emblem of Jesus Christ, the Creator and Redeemer of the human race; and that it should signify him who is the basis of all things; who upholds all by the word of his power; without whom nothing is stable, nothing fruitful; from whom alone the water of life proceeds; and in whose name only is salvation. And that rock (in the wilderness) was Christ! and it is the only remaining emblem of him in creation.
entries.9dbc08cf7667b5e18a5a03106fc52f6b8ba940eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen22166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22167" type="x-p"/> That they might observe his statutes - That they might be properly instructed, and properly disciplined. This is the end proposed by Divine revelation: men are to be made wise unto salvation, and then to be brought under the yoke of obedience. He who is not conformed to God's word shall not enter into Christ's kingdom.  <chapter eID="Ps.105"/> <div eID="gen22167" type="x-p"/>

entries.035e4b72de2554e7e495a8ff42631cd12e11de6a: <div eID="gen10009" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Thanksgiving Hymn in Honour of God Who Is Attested in the Earliest History of Israel</title> <div sID="gen10010" type="x-p"/> We have here another Psalm closing with <hi type="italic">Hallelujah</hi>, which opens the series of the <hi type="italic">Hodu</hi>-Psalms. Such is the name we give only to Psalms which begin with הודו (Ps 105, Ps 107, Ps 118, Ps 136), just as we call those which begin with הללויה (Ps 106, <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1">Psa 111:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.117.1-Ps.117.2">Psa 117:1-2</reference>, Ps 135, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.1">Psa 146:1</reference>) <hi type="italic">Hallelujah</hi>-Psalms (<hi type="italic">alleluiatici</hi>). The expression להלּל וּלהודות, which frequently occurs in the books of Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah, points to these two kinds of Psalms, or at least to their key-notes. <div eID="gen10010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10011" type="x-p"/> The festival song which David, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.7">1Ch 16:7</reference>, handed over to Asaph and his brethren for musical execution at the setting down of the Ark and the opening of divine service on Zion, is, so far as its first part is concerned (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.8-1Chr.16.22">1Ch 16:8-22</reference>), taken from our Psalm (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.1">Psa 105:1</reference>), which is then followed by <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> as a second part, and is closed with <reference osisRef="Ps.106.1">Psa 106:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference>-48. Hitzig regards the festival song in the chronicler as the original, and the respective parallels in the Psalms as “layers or shoots.” “The chronicler,” says he, “there produces with labour, and therefore himself seeking foreign aid, a song for a past that is dead.” But the transition from <reference osisRef="Ps.105.22">Psa 105:22</reference> to <reference osisRef="Ps.105.23">Psa 105:23</reference> and from <reference osisRef="Ps.105.33">Psa 105:33</reference> to <reference osisRef="Ps.105.34">Psa 105:34</reference>, so devoid of connection, the taking over of the verse out of Ps 106 referring to the Babylonian exile into <reference osisRef="Ps.105.35">Psa 105:35</reference>, and even of the doxology of the Fourth Book, regarded as an integral part of the Psalm, into <reference osisRef="Ps.105.36">Psa 105:36</reference>, refute that perversion of the right relation which has been attempted in the interest of the Maccabaean Psalms. That festival song in the chronicler, as has been shown again very recently by Riehm and Köhler, is a compilation of parts of songs already at hand, arranged for a definite purpose. Starting on the assumption that the Psalms as a whole are Davidic (just as all the Proverbs are Salomonic), because David called the poetry of the Psalms used in religious worship into existence, the attempt is made in that festival song to represent the opening of the worship on Zion, at that time in strains belonging to the Davidic Psalms. <div eID="gen10011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10012" type="x-p"/> So far as the subject-matter is concerned, Psalms 105 attaches itself to the Asaph Ps 78, which recapitulates the history of Israel. The recapitulation here, however, is made not with any didactic purpose, but with the purpose of forming a hymn, and does not come down beyond the time of Moses and Joshua. Its source is likewise the Tôra as it now lies before us. The poet epitomizes what the Tôra narrates, and clothes it in a poetic garb.
entries.e1f033c1546f922efcb792e78c64132b2f8e0924: <reference osisRef="Ps.105.1-Ps.105.6">Psa 105:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen10012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10013" type="x-p"/> Invitation to the praise - praise that resounds far and wide among the peoples - of the God who has become manifest wondrously in the deeds and words connected with the history of the founding of Israel. הודה לה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.33.2">Psa 33:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.2">Psa 75:2</reference>, of a praising and thankful confession offered to God; קרא בשׁם ה, to call with the name of Jahve, i.e., to call upon it, of an audible, solemn attestation of God in prayer and in discourse (Symmachus, κηρύσσετε). The joy of heart<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> of ישׂמח with the following <hi type="italic">Legarme</hi> seems here to be of equal value with <hi type="italic">Zakeph</hi>, 1Ch 16:10.</note> that is desired is the condition of a joyous opening of the mouth and Israel’s own stedfast turning towards Jahve, the condition of all salutary result; for it is only His “strength” that breaks through all dangers, and His “face” that lightens up all darkness. משׁפּטי־פּיו, as <reference osisRef="Ps.105.7">Psa 105:7</reference> teaches, are God’s judicial utterances, which have been executed without any hindrance, more particularly in the case of the Egyptians, their Pharaoh, and their gods. The chronicler has פּיהוּ and זרע ישׂראל, which is so far unsuitable as one does not know whether עבדו is to be referred to “Israel” the patriarch, or to the “seed of Israel,” the nation; the latter reference would be deutero-Isaianic. In both texts the lxx reads עבדו (ye His servants).
entries.ed4e715354a4962456271814dbca51169a4badee: <reference osisRef="Ps.105.7-Ps.105.11">Psa 105:7-11</reference> <div eID="gen10013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10014" type="x-p"/> The poet now begins himself to do that to which he encourages Israel. Jahve is Israel’s God: His righteous rule extends over the whole earth, whilst His people experience His inviolable faithfulness to His covenant. יהוה in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.105.7">Psa 105:7</reference></hi> is in apposition to הוּא, for the God who bears this name is as a matter of course the object of the song of praise. זכר is the perfect of practically pledges certainty (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.111.5">Psa 111:5</reference>, where we find instead the future of confident prospect). The chronicler has זכרוּ instead (lxx again something different: μνημονεύωμεν); but the object is not the demanding but the promissory side of the covenant, so that consequently it is not Israel’s remembering but God’s that is spoken of. He remembers His covenant in all time to come, so that exile and want of independence as a state are only temporary, exceptional conditions. צוּה has its radical signification here, to establish, institute, Psa 111:9. לאלף דּור (in which expression דור is a specifying accusative) is taken from Deu 7:9. And since דּבר is the covenant word of promise, it can be continued אשׁר כּרת; and Hag 2:5 (vid., Köhler thereon) shows that אשׁר is not joined to בריתו over <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.105.8">Psa 105:8</reference></hi>. וּשׁבוּעתו, however, is a second object to זכר (since דּבר with what belongs to it as an apposition is out of the question). It is the oath on Moriah (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.16">Gen 22:16</reference>) that is meant, which applied to Abraham and his seed. לישׂחק (chronicler ליצחק), as in <reference osisRef="Amos.7.9">Amo 7:9</reference>; Jer 33:26. To זכר is appended ויּעמרדה; the suffix, intended as neuter, points to what follows, viz., this, that Canaan shall be Israel’s hereditary land. From Abraham and Isaac we come to Jacob-Israel, who as being the father of the twelve is the twelve-tribe nation itself that is coming into existence; hence the plural can alternate with the singular in Psa 105:11. את־ארץ כּנען (chronicler, without the את) is an accusative of the object, and חבל נחלתכם accusative of the predicate: the land of Canaan as the province of your own hereditary possession measured out with a measuring line (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.55">Psa 78:55</reference>).
entries.cab434b86d39019d319540a3643ab1d5ef447824: <reference osisRef="Ps.105.12-Ps.105.15">Psa 105:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen10014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10015" type="x-p"/> The poet now celebrates the divine preservation which had sway over the small beginnings of Israel, when it made the patriarchs proof against harm on their wanderings. “Men of number” are such as can be easily counted, vid., the confessions in <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Gen 34:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">Deu 26:5</reference>; ויּתהלּכוּ places the claim upon the hospitality at one time of this people and at another time of that people in the connection with it of cause and effect. כּמעט, as a small number, only such a small number, signifies, as being virtually an adjective: inconsiderable, insignificant, worthless (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.20">Pro 10:20</reference>). בּהּ refers to Canaan. In <reference osisRef="Ps.105.13">Psa 105:13</reference> the way in which the words גּוי and עם alternate is instructive: the former signifies the nation, bound together by a common origin, language, country, and descent; the latter the people, bound together by unity of government.<note placement="foot">For this reason a king says עמּי, not גּויי; and גּוי only occurs twice with a suffix, which refers to Jahve (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.5">Psa 106:5</reference>; Zep 2:9); for this reason גּוי, frequently side by side with עם, is the nobler word, e.g., in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">Deu 32:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jer 2:11</reference>; for this reason עם is frequently added to גּוי as a dignitative predicate, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.13">Exo 33:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deu 4:6</reference>; and for this reason גּוים and עם ה are used antithetically.</note> <div eID="gen10015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10016" type="x-p"/> The apodosis does not begin until Psa 105:14. It is different in connection with בּהיותכם in the text of the chronicler, and in this passage in the Psalter of the Syriac version, according to which <reference osisRef="Ps.105.12">Psa 105:12</reference> ought to be jointed to the preceding group. The variation ומממלכה instead of מממלכה is of no consequence; but לאישׁ (to any one whomsoever) instead of אדם, in connection with הניח, restores the current mode of expression (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Ecc 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.11">2Sa 16:11</reference>; Hos 4:17) instead of one which is without support elsewhere, but which follows the model of נתן, נטשׁ, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.28">Gen 31:28</reference> (cf. <hi type="italic">supra</hi> p. 171); whilst on the other hand ובנביאי instead of ולנביאי substitutes an expression that cannot be supported for the current one (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.9">Gen 19:9</reference>; Rth 1:21). In <reference osisRef="Ps.105.14">Psa 105:14</reference> the poet has the three histories of the preservation of the wives of the patriarchs in his mind, viz., of Sarah in Egypt (Gen. 12), and of Sarah and of Rebekah both in Philistia (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.1-Ps.20.9">Psa 20:1-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1-Ps.26.12">Psa 26:1-12</reference>, cf. especially <reference osisRef="Ps.26.11">Psa 26:11</reference>). In the second instance God declares the patriarch to be a “prophet” (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>). The one mention has reference to this and the other to Gen. 17, where Abram is set apart to be the father of peoples and kings, and Sarai to be a princess. They are called משׁיהים (a passive form) as eing God-chosen princes, and נביאים (an intensive active form, from נבא, root נב, to divulge), not as being inspired ones (Hupfeld), but as being God’s spokesmen (cf. Exo 7:1. with Exo 4:15.), therefore as being the recipients and mediators of a divine revelation.
entries.2165cd0796fc15460123647e6b49299f4faf179d: <reference osisRef="Ps.105.16-Ps.105.24">Psa 105:16-24</reference> “To call up a famine” is also a prose expression in 2Ki 8:1. <hi type="italic">To break the staff of bread </hi>(i.e., the staff which bread is to man) is a very old metaphor, Lev 26:26. That the selling of Joseph was, providentially regarded, a “sending before,” he himself says in Gen 45:5. <reference osisRef="Ps.102.24">Psa 102:24</reference> throws light upon the meaning of ענּה ב. The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> רגלו is just as much without any occasion to justify it as עינו in <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.8">Ecc 4:8</reference> (for עיניו). The statement that iron came upon his soul is intended to say that he had to endure in iron fetters sufferings that threatened his life. Most expositors take בּרזל as equivalent to בּבּרזל, but Hitzig rightly takes נפשׁו as an object, following the Targum; for ברזל as a name of an iron fetter<note placement="foot">Also in ancient Arabic <hi type="italic">firzil</hi> (after the Aramaic פרזלא) directly signifies an iron fetter (and the large smith’s shears for cutting the iron), whence the <hi type="italic">verb. denom</hi>. Arab. <hi type="italic">farzala , c. acc. pers.,</hi> to put any one into iron chains. Iron is called בּרזל from בּרז, to pierce, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">ḥdı̂d</hi>, as being the material of which pointed tools are made.</note> can change its gender, as do, e.g., צפון as a name of the north wind, and כבוד as a name of the soul. The imprisonment (so harsh at the commencement) lasted over ten years, until at last Joseph’s word cam to pass, viz., the word concerning this exaltation which had been revealed to him in dreams (<reference osisRef="Gen.42.9">Gen 42:9</reference>). According to <reference osisRef="Ps.107.20">Psa 107:20</reference>, דברו appears to be the word of Jahve, but then one would expect from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.105.19">Psa 105:19</reference></hi> a more parallel turn of expression. What is meant is Joseph’s open-hearted word concerning his visions, and אמרת ה is the revelation of God conveying His promises, which came to him in the same form, which had to try, to prove, and to purify him (צרף as in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference>, and frequently), inasmuch as he was not to be raised to honour without having in a state of deep abasement proved a faithfulness that wavered not, and a confidence that knew no despair. The divine “word” is conceived of as a living effectual power, as in Psa 119:50. The representation of the exaltation begins, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.41.14">Gen 41:14</reference>, with שׁלח־מלך<note placement="foot">Here שׁלח is united by <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> with the following word, to which it hurries on, whereas in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.28">Psa 105:28</reference> it has its own accent, a circumstance to which the Masora has directed attention in the apophthegm: שׁלוחי דמלכא זריזין שׁלוחי דחשׁוכא מתינין (the emissaries of the king are in haste, those of darkness are tardy); vid., Baer, <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 22.</note> and follows <reference osisRef="Gen.41.39-Gen.41.41">Gen 41:39-41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.44">Gen 41:44</reference>, very closely as to the rest, according to which בּנפשׁו is a collateral definition to לאסּר (with an orthophonic <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>.) in the sense of בּרצונו: by his soul, i.e., by virtue of his will (vid., <hi type="italic">Psychology</hi>, S. 202; tr. p. 239). In consequence of this exaltation of Joseph, Jacob-Israel came then into Egypt, and sojourned there as in a protecting house of shelter (concerning גּוּר, vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 414). Egypt is called (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.23">Psa 105:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.27">Psa 105:27</reference>) the land of <hi type="italic">Chaam</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.51">Psa 78:51</reference>; according to Plutarch, in the vernacular the black land, from the dark ashy grey colouring which the deposited mud of the Nile gives to the ground. There Israel became a powerful, numerous people (<reference osisRef="Exod.1.7">Exo 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">Deu 26:5</reference>), greater than their oppressors.
entries.7a477194eeba155948f1eca669faea93efef7ec1: <reference osisRef="Ps.105.25-Ps.105.38">Psa 105:25-38</reference> <div eID="gen10016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10017" type="x-p"/> Narration of the Exodus out of Egypt after the plagues that went forth over that land. <reference osisRef="Ps.105.25">Psa 105:25</reference> tells how the Egyptians became their “oppressors.” It was indirectly God’s work, inasmuch as He gave increasing might to His people, which excited their jealousy. The craft reached its highest pitch in the weakening of the Israelites that was aimed at by killing all the male children that were born. דּברי signifies facts, instances, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.65.4">Psa 65:4</reference>; Psa 145:5. Here, too, as in Ps 78, the miraculous judgments of the ten plagues to not stand in exactly historical order. The poet begins with the ninth, which was the most distinct self-representation of divine wrath, viz., the darkness (<reference osisRef="Exod.10.21-Exod.10.29">Exo 10:21-29</reference>): <hi type="italic">shā'lach chō'shech</hi>. The former word (שׁלח) has an orthophonic <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> by the final syllable, which warns the reader audibly to utter the guttural of the toneless final syllable, which might here be easily slurred over. The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. החשׁיך has its causative signification here, as also in <reference osisRef="Jer.13.16">Jer 13:16</reference>; the contracted mode of writing with <hi type="italic">i</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">ı̂</hi> may be occasioned by the <hi type="italic">Waw convers.</hi> <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.105.28">Psa 105:28</reference></hi> cannot be referred to the Egyptians; for the expression would be a mistaken one for the final compliance, which was wrung from them, and the interrogative way of taking it: <hi type="italic">nonne rebellarunt</hi>, is forced: the cancelling of the לא, however (lxx and Syriac), makes the thought halting. Hitzig proposes ולא שׁמרו: they observed not His words; but this, too, sounds flat and awkward when said of the Egyptians. The subject will therefore be the same as the subject of שׂמוּ; and of Moses and Aaron, in contrast to the behaviour at <hi type="italic">Mê - Merı̂bah</hi> (Num 20:24; Num 27:14; cf. 1Ki 13:21, 1Ki 13:26), it is said that this time they rebelled not against the words (<hi type="italic">Kerî</hi>, without any ground: the word) of God, but executed the terrible commands accurately and willingly. From the ninth plague the poet in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.29">Psa 105:29</reference> passes over to the first (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.14-Exod.7.25">Exo 7:14-25</reference>), viz., the red blood is appended to the black darkness. The second plague follows, viz., the frogs (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.1-Exod.8.15">Exo 8:1-15</reference>); <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.105.20">Psa 105:20</reference></hi> looks as though it were stunted, but neither has the lxx read any ויבאו (ויעלו), Ex. 7:28. In <reference osisRef="Ps.105.31">Psa 105:31</reference> he next briefly touches upon the fourth plague, viz., the gad-fly, ערב, lxx κυνόμυια (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.20-Exod.8.32">Exo 8:20-32</reference>, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.78.45">Psa 78:45</reference>), and the third (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.16-Exod.8.19">Exo 8:16-19</reference>), viz., the gnats, which are passed over in Ps 78. From the third plague the poet in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.32">Psa 105:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.33">Psa 105:33</reference> takes a leap over to the seventh, viz., the hail (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.13-Exod.9.35">Ex 9:13-35</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Ps.105.32">Psa 105:32</reference> he has <reference osisRef="Exod.9.24">Exo 9:24</reference> before his mind, according to which masses of fire descended with the hail; and in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.33">Psa 105:33</reference> (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.47">Psa 78:47</reference>) he fills in the details of Exo 9:25. The seventh plague is followed by the eighth in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.34">Psa 105:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.35">Psa 105:35</reference>, viz., the locust (<reference osisRef="Exod.10.1-Exod.10.20">Ex 10:1-20</reference>), to which ילק (the grasshopper) is the parallel word here, just as חסיל (the cricket) is in Psa 78:46. The expression of innumerableness is the same as in Psa 104:25. The fifth plague, viz., the pestilence, murrain (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.1-Exod.9.7">Exo 9:1-7</reference>), and the sixth, viz., שׁחין, boils (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.8-Exod.9.12">Exo 9:8-12</reference>), are left unmentioned; and the tenth plague closes, viz., the smiting of the first-born (Exo 11:1.), which <reference osisRef="Ps.105.36">Psa 105:36</reference> expresses in the Asaphic language of Psa 78:51. Without any mention of the institution of the Passover, the tenth plague is followed by the departure with the vessels of silver and gold asked for from the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.35">Exo 12:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.11.2">Exo 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.3.22">Exo 3:22</reference>). The Egyptians were glad to get rid of the people whose detention threatened them with total destruction (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.33">Exo 12:33</reference>). The poet here draws from <reference osisRef="Isa.5.27">Isa 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.31">Isa 14:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.13">Isa 63:13</reference>, and Exo 15:16. The suffix of שׁבטיו refers to the chief subject of the assertion, viz., to God, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.122.4">Psa 122:4</reference>, although manifestly enough the reference to Israel is also possible (Num 24:2).
entries.342704c25ffcd66e0bf6886b468eedff5ba232e0: <reference osisRef="Ps.105.39-Ps.105.45">Psa 105:39-45</reference> <div eID="gen10017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10018" type="x-p"/> Now follows the miraculous guidance through the desert to the taking possession of Canaan. The fact that the cloud (ענן, root ען, to meet, to present itself to view, whence the Arabic <hi type="italic">‛ănăn</hi>, the visible outward side of the vault of heaven) by day, and becoming like fire by night, was their guide (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.21">Exo 13:21</reference>), is left out of consideration in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.105.39">Psa 105:39</reference></hi>. With למסך we are not to associate the idea of a covering against foes, Exo 14:19., but of a covering from the smiting sun, for פּרשׁ (<reference osisRef="Exod.40.19">Exo 40:19</reference>), as in Isa 4:5., points to the idea of a canopy. In connection with the sending of the quails the tempting character of the desire is only momentarily dwelt upon, the greater emphasis is laid on the omnipotence of the divine goodness which responded to it. שׁאלוּ is to be read instead of שׁאל, the w before w having been overlooked; and the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> writes and points שׂליו (like סתיו, עניו) in order to secure the correct pronunciation, after the analogy of the plural termination יו-. The bread of heaven (Psa 78:24.) is the manna. In <reference osisRef="Ps.105.41">Psa 105:41</reference> the giving of water out of the rock at Rephidim and at Kadesh are brought together; the expression corresponds better to the former instance (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.6">Exo 17:6</reference>, cf. Num 20:11). הלכוּ refers to the waters, and נהר for כּנּהרות, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.16">Psa 78:16</reference>, is, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Psa 22:14</reference>, an equation instead of a comparison. In this miraculous escort the patriarchal promise moves on towards its fulfilment; the holy word of promise, and the stedfast, proved faith of Abraham - these were the two motives. The second את is, like the first, a sign of the object, not a preposition (lxx, Targum), in connection with which <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.105.42">Psa 105:42</reference></hi> would be a continuation of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.105.42">Psa 105:42</reference></hi>, dragging on without any parallelism. Joy and exulting are mentioned as the mood of the redeemed ones with reference to the festive joy displayed at the Red Sea and at Sinai. By <reference osisRef="Ps.105.43">Psa 105:43</reference> one is reminded of the same descriptions of the antitype in Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">Isa 35:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.11">Isa 51:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.12">Isa 55:12</reference>, just as <reference osisRef="Ps.105.41">Psa 105:41</reference> recalls Isa 48:21. “The lands of the heathen” are the territories of the tribes of Canaan. עמל is equivalent to יגיע in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.14">Isa 45:14</reference> : the cultivated ground, the habitable cities, and the accumulated treasures. Israel entered upon the inheritance of these peoples in every direction. As an independent people upon ground that is theirs by inheritance, keeping the revealed law of their God, was Israel to exhibit the pattern of a holy nation moulded after the divine will; and, as the beginning of the Psalm shows, to unite the peoples to themselves and their God, the God of redemption, by the proclamation of the redemption which has fallen to their own lot.  <chapter eID="Ps.105"/> <div eID="gen10018" type="x-p"/>

entries.c78f1dac934d148931665a52041b05ed7bba1f4b:
PSALM 105
The Psalmist magnifies the singular grace of God displayed in selecting and freely adopting one people from amongst all nations of the world. To show that it was not in word only that he had made a covenant with Abraham and his offspring, God did not cease, after having delivered them from Egypt, to confer upon them innumerable benefits; and his design in this was, that those who had been delivered might on their part faithfully keep his covenant, and devote themselves unfeignedly to his service.
This psalm has no title in the Hebrew or Chaldee, but in the Vulgate, Septuagint, Æthiopic, and Arabic versions, the hallelujah which concludes the preceding psalm is prefixed as the inscription. The first fifteen verses correspond with the first part of a song of thanksgiving, which David composed to be sung after the ark had been brought from Obed-edom to Zion. — See 1 Chronicles 15:8-22. Hence some conclude, that David was its inspired penman, and that he probably enlarged it at some subsequent period of his history, that it might supply a more complete commemoration of God’s signal and extraordinary goodness towards the Israelites from the days of Abraham to their final settlement in the land of Canaan; while others conclude, that it was enlarged by some Hebrew bard, at the restoration of the Jews from the Babylonish captivity. This psalm bears a strong resemblance to the 78th, as well in the subject as in the style, except perhaps that the diction here is rather of a more simple cast.
Psalm 105:1-5
1. Praise ye Jehovah; invoke his name: announce his works among the peoples. 2. Sing ye to him: sing psalms to him: speak ye of all his wonders. 3. Rejoice ye in his holy name:
In the French version it is, “Praise ye his holy name.” Hammond, agreeably to this, would read, “Praise ye the name of his holiness;” thinking that ב, beth, in, is a pleonasm.
let the heart of those who seek Jehovah rejoice. 4. Seek ye Jehovah, and his strength: seek his face continually. 5. Remember the marvelous works which he hath performed; his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth.
 
1 Praise ye Jehovah, etc. The object of these opening words simply is, that the offspring of Abraham should place all their blessedness in the free adoption of God. It was indeed a blessing not to be despised that they had been created men, that they had been cherished in the world by God’s fatherly care, and that they had received sustenance at his hand; but it was a far more distinguished privilege to have been chosen to be his peculiar people. While the whole human race are condemned in Adam, the condition of the Israelites was so different from all other nations, as to give them ground to boast, that they were consecrated to God. This is the reason why the prophet heaps together so many words in commendation of this grace. He does not treat of the government of the whole world as he did in the preceding psalm, but he celebrates the fatherly favor which God had manifested towards the children of Israel. He indeed names in general his works, and his wonders, but he limits both to that spiritual covenant by which God made choice of a church, that might lead on earth a heavenly life. He does not intend to include as among these wonders, that the sun, moon, and stars, daily rise to give light to the world, that the earth produces its fruit in its seasons, that every living creature is supplied with abundance of all good things for its food, and that the human family are liberally provided with so many conveniences; but he celebrates the sovereign grace of God, by which he chose for himself from amongst the lost race of Adam a small portion to whom he might show himself to be a father. Accordingly, he enjoins them to rejoice in the name of God, and to call upon him; a privilege by which the Church alone is distinguished. Whence it follows, that this language is addressed to none but true believers, whom God would have to glory in his name, since he has taken them under his special protection.

                  <ns0:p n="38">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:496" />38. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 12. 33.</ns0:note> Egypt was glad when they departed: for the fear of them <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Of the Israelites, left God for their sakes should destroy them.</ns0:note> fell upon them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="39">39. <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Exod. 13. 21.</ns0:note> He spread a cloud for a covering <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To protect them from the heat of the Sun, which in that hot and open Country had otherwise been intolerable to them, especially in so long a Journey.</ns0:note> and fire to give light in the night.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="40">40. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 16. 12, &c.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>The people</ns0:hi> asked, and he brought quails <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He speaks of the first giving of Quails, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 16. 13. which God gave them as a refreshment, notwithstanding their Sin in desiring them, which he graciously pardoned; and not of that second giving of Quails, which God gave them in judgment, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 11. and therefore would not have been num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bered here amongst Gods favours vouchsafed to them.</ns0:note>: and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Psal. 78. 24, 25.</ns0:note> satisfied them with the bread of heaven <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">With Manna which came out of the Air, which is commonly called <ns0:hi>Heaven.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
